Yes.

**Strongest “yes” speech:**

Honorable judges, my opponents, and everyone listening:

I am not here to defend a world in which torture is routine, legal, or convenient. I am not here to defend abuse, cruelty, or the corruption of institutions. I am here to answer one terrible question: if a million human beings will die unless we extract one piece of information from one person in our custody, and torture is genuinely the only way to obtain that information, are we morally permitted — and perhaps morally required — to do it?

I say: yes.

This is not a normal case. Normal cases are what we usually talk about: policing, counterterrorism, intelligence, long-term investigations. In normal cases, torture is wrong. It degrades the state, it corrupts the interrogator, it produces false confessions, and it treats persons as means. I grant all of that. But the scenario before us is not normal. It is the exception so extreme that it tests the limits of our principles.

The facts are these: a terrorist is in custody. He knows where the bomb is. A million people will die. Time is short. Every other method has failed. Torture is the only way. Under those conditions, the moral calculus changes completely.

My argument rests on three pillars: the duty to prevent catastrophic harm, the impossibility of absolute duties when lives are at stake, and the necessity of constrained moral decision-making even in tragedy.

First, we have a duty to rescue.

If a child is drowning and you can save the child by breaking a window, you do not stand by the principle that windows must not be broken. If a car is about to run over a group of pedestrians and you can stop it by damaging someone else’s property, you do not refuse because property rights are important. In both cases, a lesser harm is permitted to prevent a greater harm.

Now scale that up. A million lives are at stake. Not ten. Not one hundred. A million. That is not an abstraction. That is mothers, children, students, workers, strangers in their homes, people who have done nothing wrong and who will die because we clung to a principle too rigidly.

When the alternative is a million deaths, inaction is not neutrality. Inaction is a choice. To refuse to use the only available means of saving a million people is, morally speaking, to choose their deaths. And that is not a position a decent person can defend without flinching — and we should flinch. But flinching does not excuse moral clarity.

Second, no moral rule is so absolute that it must survive a collision with genocide-scale death.

Opponents will say: torture violates human dignity. They will say: we do not become like the enemy when we torture. They will say: some lines must not be crossed.

I respect those instincts. But they are not self-executing. When two duties collide, one must yield. We may have a duty not to torture. But we also have a duty not to stand by while a million innocent people are killed. If both duties cannot be fulfilled, we must choose the lesser moral evil.

And here, the lesser evil is clear.

The violation inflicted on one person through coercive interrogation is grave. But the violation inflicted on a million people through their preventable murder is incomparably greater. To say otherwise is to make human life arbitrary: a million lives matter, but not enough; one person’s dignity matters, but more than a million lives. That is not moral consistency. That is moral evasion.

Third, this justification only works if it is narrow, exceptional, and controlled.

I want to be very clear: this argument does not justify torture as policy. It does not justify torture in ordinary investigations. It does not justify torture when there is uncertainty, when there is time, when there are alternative methods, or when the expected number of lives saved is small.

The justification here depends on strict conditions:

1. **The person must actually know where the bomb is.**  
   If we are not certain, the justification collapses. We cannot torture based on suspicion.

2. **The harm must be imminent and catastrophic.**  
   This is not a theoretical bomb. It is a bomb that will kill a million people.

3. **Every lesser means must have failed.**  
   We are not at the first resort. We are at the last.

4. **The use of force must be limited to obtaining the specific information needed.**  
   This is not punishment. It is not revenge. It is not interrogation for its own sake. It is a tragic attempt to save lives.

5. **There must be accountability.**  
   Those who authorize and carry it out must be able to show that the conditions were real, not fabricated. After the fact, they must answer for their actions.

This is not a license to abuse. It is an emergency exception so narrow that most real-world cases would not meet it. And that is precisely why it is defensible: it does not open the floodgates. It addresses the impossible.

Now my opponents will say this leads to a slippery slope. They will say: once you permit torture in one case, the state will permit it in another. They will say the rule will expand, the justification will become routine, and eventually no one will be safe.

I answer: the danger of the slippery slope is real, but it is not a reason to let a million people die. The answer to abuse is not the absence of moral seriousness; it is stronger safeguards, independent review, transparent accountability, and a legal system that recognizes the exception without normalizing it.

If we refuse to face the hardest case, we do not protect the rule of law. We reveal that our principles are too brittle to survive reality.

And let me speak to the deeper moral question: what kind of society do we become?

My opponents will say we become a society that tortures. I agree: we become a society that has faced an impossible choice and chosen the lesser horror. We become a society that does not pretend innocence can preserve life. We become a society that accepts that sometimes moral agents must bear the stain of doing something terrible in order to prevent something worse.

But is that so different from war? We do not usually say that war is good. We say it is sometimes necessary. We do not celebrate the soldier who kills. We honor the soldier who acts under dire necessity. We do not pretend that killing is clean. But we recognize that sometimes, to save lives, we must impose harm.

This case is simply that recognition pushed to its limit.

Imagine the faces of those million people. Not as a number, but as people. The student waking up to class. The parent going to work. The elderly person in their home. The child who will never grow up. All of them are real in this scenario. All of them are preventable losses. And if we have the power to save them, if we truly have the power, then to refuse is not purity. It is cowardice dressed up as principle.

I do not say this lightly. I do not say this with celebration. I say it with the full weight of what it means to choose the lesser evil.

If torture is truly the only way, and a million lives truly depend on it, then the morally defensible answer is yes — not because torture is good, not because the terrorist deserves suffering, not because we enjoy power over the captive, but because the alternative is a catastrophe so immense that our failure to act would make us complicit in the deaths of a million innocent people.

So my position is this:

**Torture is ordinarily wrong. It is dangerous. It must be prohibited in all but the most extreme circumstances. But in this scenario, where the facts are certain and the alternative is a million deaths, the strongest moral argument is that it is justified as a last resort, under strict limits, with accountability, and with the full horror of the choice recognized.**

We should not wish this case upon anyone. We should not make it routine. We should not excuse it after the fact. But we should not pretend that principle means standing still while a million people die.

If the bomb can be stopped only this way, then yes — we must.
